title: Samuel HaNagid
hook: poet, scholar, and vizier of Granada

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hasdai ibn Shaprut, the court doctor in Córdoba who backed scholars and poets. Your line was use your place. Today, a man who held a place and a pen at once.

A small spice shop stands near a great man's house in Málaga. The shopkeeper is a refugee, a Jew who fled the fighting in Córdoba. He has beautiful handwriting and better Arabic, so a servant from the great house keeps asking him to write letters for her master. The letters are so good that the master, a vizier to the king of Granada, wants to know who is writing them. That, at least, is how the medieval chronicle tells it. The shopkeeper is Samuel ibn Naghrela. He'll become the king's chief minister, lead armies, and write Hebrew poems about all of it. Jews will call him HaNagid.
screen: `A SPICE SHOP IN MÁLAGA.` → `LETTERS FOR THE VIZIER.` → `A REFUGEE CALLED TO COURT.`

segments.voice: Start with the title. Nagid is a Hebrew word the Bible uses for a leader. When God tells Samuel the prophet to anoint Saul, the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation renders it: "thou shalt anoint him to be prince over My people Israel." Prince there is nagid. So HaNagid means the leader, the title Jews gave the man who led their community in Granada. Now the double life. In the Muslim kingdom of Granada, Samuel rose from secretary to vizier, the king's chief minister, and commanded its armies in the field. And he wrote poems the whole time. War poems, written on campaign, thanking God for being spared in battle. Poems of wine, gardens and friendship, in the style of Arabic poetry. Poems about death, sitting with the bones of old kings and wondering where they went. Poems to his young son, teaching him to love learning. He gathered them into books named after biblical ones: a son of Psalms, a son of Proverbs, a son of Ecclesiastes. Meanwhile he wrote on Jewish law, supported students, and paid for copies of books for those who couldn't afford them. Statesman and poet, general and scholar. One person can hold two callings and let each feed the other. The pen made him a minister. The ministry gave the pen something to say.
screen: `NAGID: A BIBLICAL WORD FOR LEADER.` · then, large: `PRINCE OVER MY PEOPLE ISRAEL.` · `VIZIER AND GENERAL.` · `POEMS FROM THE BATTLEFIELD.`

segments.voice: Name one thing you're good at for work or duty, organizing, fixing, caring for someone, numbers, and one thing you love that nobody pays you for, singing, cooking, drawing, walking. Hold them side by side, and let one small way they could help each other come to mind. If you pray, you can give thanks in your own words for both gifts.
Samuel HaNagid. Samuel the leader: a refugee shopkeeper who became vizier of Granada, led its armies, and wrote Hebrew poems all the way. Today's word.
Your line: poet and statesman. A refugee's handwriting ended up shaping a kingdom. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Samuel HaNagid's Hebrew poems are studied as part of the golden age of Hebrew poetry in Spain, and his title, Nagid, is remembered as the name for the leader of a Jewish community.
